summary: Gives replacement text and a replacement figure for the Very Distant Host specification in BBN Report 1822, which defined how a Host connects to an IMP. Readers were asked to file it with their copy of Report 1822 until that document was next updated.

plainLanguage.summary: A rulebook had a mistake in one drawing and paragraph. This note hands out the fixed page to tape into your copy.

questions: how do you know if an imp connection is dead
subtitle: Corrected specification for connecting distant hosts to IMPs.

tldr.problem: The Very Distant Host specification in BBN Report 1822 contained an error in a diagram and accompanying text that described how hosts could connect to IMPs.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 547 provides replacement text and a corrected diagram (Figure F-4, the Control Word Format) along with an algorithm describing how IMPs and distant hosts detect when their connection is alive or dead.
tldr.outcome: Sites could file this RFC with their copy of Report 1822 until that document was updated, correcting the specification without requiring a full revision of the 1822 document.

today: RFC 547 is one of the earliest errata distributions on the ARPANET. It illustrates how the network community handled specification corrections before formal errata processes existed.

sections.title: The Fix
sections.content: RFC 547 provides replacement text and a corrected figure for the Very Distant Host specification section of BBN Report 1822, which defines how a Host connects to an IMP (Interface Message Processor). The document was authored by D. Walden at BBN and sent to the network community asking them to incorporate these corrections with their copies of Report 1822 until that document underwent its next full revision.
sections.plainLanguage: Here is the corrected page that goes into your copy of the rulebook about connecting computers to the network.

sections.title: The Control Word Format
sections.content: The corrected Figure F-4 shows the Control Word Format for IMP-Host communication. The diagram identifies key fields and bits including the LAST PACKET bit, PACKET ODD/EVEN bit, PACKET WORD COUNT (6 bits), HOST/IMP bit, CHANNEL ZERO ACKNOWLEDGE bit, CHANNEL ONE ACKNOWLEDGEMENT bit, CHANNEL NUMBER, the HELLO/I-HEARD-YOU bit, SPECIAL PACKET bit, and unused bits.
sections.plainLanguage: A control word is like a label at the top of a message between a computer and the network hardware, telling what kind of message it is and where it should go.

sections.title: Detecting Live and Dead Connections
sections.content: The replacement text defines an algorithm for deciding whether the circuit between an IMP and a very distant Host is alive or dead. Both the IMP and Host independently send HELLO packets (special packets with the HELLO/I-HEARD-YOU bit set to zero) every r seconds. When either receives a HELLO packet, they must promptly send an I-HEARD-YOU packet in acknowledgement. If either side sends more than t HELLO packets without receiving an I-HEARD-YOU acknowledgement, the circuit is declared dead. After a waiting period of 2*t*r seconds, the party that declared the line dead attempts to bring it back up by sending HELLO packets every r seconds until k HELLO packets in a row are acknowledged with I-HEARD-YOU packets, at which point the line is declared alive again and regular data packets can be exchanged.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides say "hello" every once in a while. If one side doesn't hear back after trying several times, it assumes the connection is broken and stops sending. After waiting a while, it tries saying hello again until it gets answers again.
